harbor.practice: Harbor uses retrieval for changing policy facts, a small SFT for the mandated answer format, and has not done continued pretraining because evaluation never showed a domain-language gap.
harbor.failure: Using fine-tuning as a substitute for a permission-aware database of changing facts.

harbor.practice: For any Harbor fine-tune, the dataset manifest records source, licence decision, content hash, language and filter outcome, and evaluation document families are excluded before training sequences are built.
harbor.failure: Assuming publicly reachable text is licensed for any training or redistribution purpose.

harbor.practice: Harbor's team used C = 6ND to show that pretraining even a 1B model on their 20B-token corpus would cost far more than adapting an existing open model, which ended the discussion.
harbor.failure: Repeating a small corpus to reach a big token count and expecting the diversity of a larger corpus.

harbor.practice: Before each Harbor SFT run, an engineer renders one example with the model's chat template and checks that only the assistant tokens carry labels.
harbor.failure: Launching a run with a mismatched chat template or wrong loss mask; training will run and still optimise the wrong tokens.

harbor.practice: Harbor's extraction reward checks schema validity and exact field values, so an empty but valid JSON object scores zero instead of full marks.
harbor.failure: Treating reward score, human preference, correctness and policy compliance as the same measurement.

harbor.practice: Harbor's one larger fine-tune ran on 8 GPUs with FSDP; the team measured 5.6× speed-up, not 8×, because of communication overhead.
harbor.failure: Expecting N GPUs to give N times the throughput.

harbor.practice: New Harbor engineers train the browser bigram model and the NumPy lab (Appendix A) in their first week, so later discussions about loss, validation and checkpoints share one picture.
harbor.failure: Reading plausible samples from a tiny memorised corpus as evidence of generalisation.
